issues.legal_issue: A finding that a religious institution exists and that some property belongs to it does not establish that every property in dispute is endowed property.
material_facts: In an earlier appeal, the Court held that the religious institution existed and that its principal building belonged to it, but remanded the case for determination of which other properties belonged to the institution.
On remand, the High Court treated all properties as belonging to the institution because the evidence did not expressly identify which properties did and did not belong to it.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred. The earlier decision left the character of the other properties for determination and did not require all properties to be treated as institution property.
issues.legal_principle: A prior finding that an institution exists, together with a finding that particular property belongs to it, does not decide the character of other properties where that question was expressly left open for further consideration.

predicates.case_on_remand: The matter is being reconsidered after a higher court remanded unresolved property-character questions.
predicates.earlier_decision_left_other_properties_u: The earlier decision established the institution or the status of particular property but left other properties for further determination.
predicates.lower_court_inferred_all_properties_were: The lower court treated every disputed property as endowed because the evidence did not expressly distinguish endowed property from other property.

issues.definition: When a matter returns on remand with the status of some properties unresolved, ambiguity in the evidence does not by itself make every disputed property endowed.

issues.legal_issue: Property held by a religious head is not endowed merely because the head acquired it while holding office or failed to distinguish it in documents from endowed property.
material_facts: The successive heads systematically conducted a money-lending business and accumulated property.
They described themselves in property documents as absolute owners and transferred property, including to members of their spiritual community, for consideration or in recognition of claims.
The evidence established little endowed property as a nucleus and did not establish that the disputed properties at issue had been dedicated or given for a charitable purpose.
The Court found that 15 items, including the building used by the institution, were institution property; it could not find that the other properties were not the personal property of the head.
issues.conclusion: A head could endow personally acquired property, but the evidence did not establish that the disputed properties beyond the 15 identified items had become institution property. The other properties were personal unless a particular item was shown to be subject to an endowment or a gift for a charitable purpose.
issues.legal_principle: The character of property depends on evidence of dedication or endowment; a religious head is legally capable of holding personal property. The Court relied on Parama Nand v. Nihal Chand, 65 I.A. 252, and Raghbir Lala v. Mohammad Said, A.I.R. 1943 P.C. 7, for the principles that succession from guru to disciple does not itself make property religious and religious profession does not make a person incapable of holding property. A head may endow personal property, but the mere absence of a distinction in property documents does not prove dedication where the evidence shows personal ownership and dealings as owner.

rule.if: property_character_is_disputed and mahant_conducted_money_lending_business and mahant_asserted_absolute_ownership and mahant_dealt_with_property_as_owner and specific_endowment_not_proved_for_property

predicates.property_character_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether property held by a religious head belongs personally to the head or to the religious institution.
predicates.mahant_conducted_money_lending_business: The religious head conducted a money-lending or similar business from which property was accumulated.
predicates.mahant_asserted_absolute_ownership: The religious head described or otherwise held himself out as the absolute owner of the property.
predicates.mahant_dealt_with_property_as_owner: The religious head transferred or otherwise dealt with the property as an owner.
predicates.specific_endowment_not_proved_for_proper: The evidence does not establish that the particular property was dedicated to the institution or given for a charitable purpose.

issues.definition: If property is disputed and the head’s business, assertions, and dealings indicate personal ownership, the property is treated as personal when no specific endowment is proved.

issues.legal_issue: Renunciation of the world and succession from guru to disciple do not, without more, make a religious head’s property institution property.
material_facts: Successive heads had renounced the world and become ascetics.
They almost uniformly nominated successors from among their disciples or disciples of disciples.
The evidence also showed personal business activity, assertions of ownership, and dealings with property as owners.
issues.conclusion: The heads’ ascetic status and the pattern of spiritual succession did not establish that their properties were institution property.
issues.legal_principle: In Parama Nand v. Nihal Chand, 65 I.A. 252, the Privy Council held that descent from guru to disciple does not necessarily change property’s secular character into a religious one. Raghbir Lala v. Mohammad Said, A.I.R. 1943 P.C. 7, recognizes that religious profession does not make a person incapable in law of holding property.

rule.if: property_character_is_disputed and holder_is_an_ascetic and succession_is_from_guru_to_disciple and no_specific_dedication_is_proved

predicates.property_character_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether property held by a religious head belongs personally to the head or to the religious institution.
predicates.holder_is_an_ascetic: The person who held the property had renounced the world and lived as an ascetic.
predicates.succession_is_from_guru_to_disciple: The property passed through a pattern of succession from a spiritual teacher to a disciple or a disciple’s disciple.
predicates.no_specific_dedication_is_proved: The evidence does not establish a dedication of the particular property to the institution or a religious purpose.

issues.definition: An ascetic holder and guru-to-disciple succession do not establish endowment where no specific dedication is proved.

issues.legal_issue: Transfers of property held personally by a religious head cannot be invalidated as transfers of institution property when the property is not proved to be endowed.
material_facts: The appeals concerned transfers made by a religious head that had been challenged as transfers of institution property.
The Court found that only 15 items were institution property and could not find that the other properties were not personal property.
The transfers of the properties in that latter class were the subject of the appeals.
issues.conclusion: The transfers of the properties not established to be institution property were upheld so far as they were before the Court in the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer cannot be challenged as an alienation of institution property when the property is not shown to belong to the institution; the Court upheld the transfers of the class of properties treated as personal. The Court did not thereby decide the validity of transfers of property found to be institution property.

predicates.appeal_challenges_invalidation_of_proper: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decision that invalidated a transfer of property.
predicates.property_not_proved_to_be_institution_pr: The evidence does not establish that the transferred property belongs to the religious institution.

issues.definition: In an appeal challenging invalidation of a transfer, a transfer is upheld when the property is not proved to belong to the institution.
